strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: existing open articulated-object datasets (PartNet-Mobility, BEHAVIOR-1K) suffer from poor visual realism, inconsistent modeling standards, or closed/encrypted assets; ArtVIP is professionally modeled with unified standards, delivering 992 articulated objects across 9 categories/37 subcategories with both visual and physical fidelity.

Evaluation spans multiple complementary axes: geometric detail (triangle counts), CLIP feature-distribution alignment with real-world images, VGGT reconstruction quality, and real-world optical motion-capture comparisons against simulated joint trajectories under controlled forces, giving reasonably convincing evidence of fidelity claims.

Novel contribution of 'modular interaction' behaviors (latching, damping, cross-asset/within-asset triggers, hover/hold) embedded directly in assets, plus an extended, physically motivated joint-drive parameterization (position/velocity-dependent stiffness and friction) that goes beyond the default PD joint model in Isaac Sim, addressing complex real-world joint dynamics like door closers.

Strong downstream validation across both imitation learning (ACT, DP on 4 real+sim manipulation tasks, plus a digital-cousin comparison against PartNet-Mobility) and reinforcement learning (EAGLE visuomotor policy with sim-to-real Pearson correlation of 0.99), showing the dataset is practically useful, not just visually appealing.

Comprehensive appendices with production guidelines, category/time breakdowns, comparisons to generative reconstruction baselines (SplArt) showing current automatic pipelines still lag far behind in mesh/material/joint quality, and open-source commitment with USD format convertible to URDF/MJCF for broad simulator compatibility.
weaknesses: Scale/generalizability trade-off: only 992 objects across 6 scenes, with some subcategories containing very few instances (e.g., 3, 6, 8 items in Table 4); the paper explicitly prioritizes quality over scale, but this limits diversity and the generalizability of downstream results.

Heavy reliance on manual professional 3D modeling (hours per asset per Table 4) raises reproducibility/scalability concerns for community extension, an issue the authors acknowledge as a limitation but do not mitigate beyond suggesting future generative methods.

Physical fidelity validation, while quantitatively presented, is based on a small number of case-study objects (drawer, microwave, oven) with limited trial counts (e.g., 10 trials) and no error bars/statistical tests, so it is unclear how representative these cases are of the full 992-asset collection.

Visual realism comparisons (t-SNE/CLIP feature overlap, qualitative renderings) are largely qualitative or visually inspected rather than using standard quantitative distributional metrics (e.g., FID), weakening the strength of the 'higher visual realism' claim.

Downstream imitation-learning success rates remain fairly low across settings (20-80%), and some plots (e.g., Fig. 6 'control group') are not clearly explained in the main text, leaving some experimental design choices ambiguous.

The paper's primary contribution is a resource/benchmark rather than a new algorithm; while the joint-dynamics formulation is a nice technical addition, the overall novelty relative to prior digital-twin/asset papers (e.g., BEHAVIOR-1K, digital-twin catalogs) is incremental in nature.
Claimed compatibility with other simulators (MuJoCo, PyBullet via URDF/MJCF conversion) is asserted but not empirically validated in the paper.
